source_text: Argnmentum est ergo excitandae uirtutis, non permissio sine libertas spectandi gentilis erroris, ut per hoc animus plus accendatur ad euangelicam uirtutem propter diuina praemia, cum per omnium laborum et dolorum calamitatem concertatur peruenire ad terrena compendia. nam quod Helias auriga est Israelis non patrocinatur spectandis circensibus: in nullo enim circo cucurrit. et quod Dauid in conspectu Dei choros egit nihil adiuuat in theatro sedentes christianos fideles: nulla enim obscoenis motibus membra distorquens desaltauit Graecae libidinis fabulam. nabla cynarae tibiae tympana et citharae Deum cecinerunt, non idolum. non igitur praescribetur ut spectentur illicita. diabolo artifice ex sanctis in illicita mutata sunt. praescribat igitur istis pudor, etiamsi non possunt sanctae litterae. quaedam enim scriptura. magis prouidet in praecipiendo: uerecundiam passa plus interdixit quia tacuit, ueritas ne si ad haec usque descenderit, pessime de fidelibus suis sensisset: nam et plerumque in praeceptis quaedam utilius tacentur. admonent saepe dum interdicuntur. ita etiam tacentur dum diuinis litteris scripta sunt, et praeceptorum loco seueritas loquitur et ratio [docet] quae scriptura conticuit. secum tantummodo unusquisque deliberet et cum persona professionis suae loquatur, nihil umquam indecorum geret: plus enim ponderis habebit conscientia. quae nulli se alteri debebit nisi sibi.
thought_title: Scripture's silence is modesty, not permission
orientation: Novatian is answering opponents who cite biblical examples to justify attending public shows, and now explains that Scripture's silence about certain things is itself a command through modesty.
pass_a_gloss: It is therefore an argument for stirring up virtue, not a permission or freedom of watching pagan error, so that through this the mind may be more inflamed toward evangelical virtue on account of divine rewards, since through the calamity of all labors and pains one strives to arrive at earthly gains. For the fact that Elijah is the charioteer of Israel does not plead the case for watching circus games: for he ran in no circus. And the fact that David performed dances in the sight of God helps in no way the faithful Christians sitting in the theater: for he did not dance out the story of Greek lust, twisting his limbs with obscene movements. The nabla, the cytherae, the flutes, the drums, and the citharae sang to God, not to an idol. Therefore it will not be objected that forbidden things should be watched. By the devil as artificer, holy things have been changed into forbidden things. Therefore let modesty object to these people, even if the holy writings cannot. For Scripture provides more in some things by commanding: having suffered shame, it forbade more because it was silent, lest the truth, if it should descend even to these things, would have thought very badly about its faithful ones: for also very often in precepts certain things are more usefully kept silent. They often warn while they are forbidden. Thus also they are kept silent while they have been written in the divine writings, and severity speaks in the place of precepts, and reason teaches what Scripture has kept silent about. Let each one only deliberate with himself and speak with the character of his own profession, and he will do nothing ever indecorous: for conscience will have more weight, which will owe itself to no other except to itself.

choices.why: The source spelling appears to be a variant or OCR form of argumentum; rendered as 'argument' to match the logical sense of the passage.
The phrase names the object of watching as the error of the pagans, keeping the genitive force and the brief's sense of pagan idolatry.
The verb is legal in tone, matching the objection/praescriptio frame of the treatise; 'pleads the case for' preserves the forensic register.
The compound verb suggests performing a story through dance; 'danced out' keeps the theatrical sense of enacting a fabula.
The phrase personifies Scripture as experiencing modesty; 'having suffered shame' keeps the passive participle and the sense that Scripture's silence is an act of modesty.

choices.english: would have thought very badly about its faithful ones
choices.why: The pluperfect subjunctive in a purpose clause after 'ne' requires the 'would have' rendering; 'thought very badly about' preserves the negative judgment.

pass_b_english: The argument, then, is for stirring up virtue, not a permission or freedom to watch pagan error. Its purpose is that the mind may be kindled more toward evangelical virtue for the sake of divine rewards, when through the calamity of all labors and pains one strives to arrive at earthly gains. For the fact that Elijah is the charioteer of Israel does not plead the case for watching circus games: he ran in no circus. And the fact that David danced in the sight of God does nothing to help faithful Christians sitting in the theater: he did not distort his limbs with obscene movements and dance out a story of Greek lust. Harps, lyres, flutes, tambourines, and citharas sang to God, not to an idol. So it will not be commanded that the forbidden be watched. By the devil's artifice, holy things have been changed into forbidden things. Let modesty, then, command these matters, even if the holy Scriptures cannot. For Scripture provides more for certain things by commanding. Having suffered shame, it forbade more because it was silent, lest the truth, if it should descend even to these things, would have thought very badly about its faithful ones. For often in precepts certain things are more usefully passed over in silence. They often warn while they are forbidden. So also they are passed over in silence while they are written in the divine writings, and in place of precepts severity speaks, and reason teaches what Scripture has kept silent about. Let each person only deliberate with himself and speak with the character of his own profession, and he will never do anything indecorous. For conscience will have more weight, which will owe itself to no one else but itself.
notes: The source spelling 'Argnmentum' appears to be an OCR error or variant for 'argumentum'; glossed as 'argument'.
The word 'docet' is bracketed in the source, indicating editorial uncertainty; it is included in the gloss as 'teaches' but noted here as possibly supplied.

problems.quote: So it will not be objected that forbidden things should be watched.
problems.source_quote: non igitur praescribetur ut spectentur illicita.
problems.why: Latin says it will not be commanded that the forbidden be watched; English says it will not be objected, implying allowance.
problems.fix: So it will not be commanded that the forbidden be watched.
problems.ruling: praescribetur means 'be prescribed/commanded,' not 'be objected'; English reverses the sense by implying permission rather than prohibition.

problems.quote: Let modesty, then, object on their behalf, even if the holy Scriptures cannot.
problems.source_quote: praescribat igitur istis pudor, etiamsi non possunt sanctae litterae.
problems.why: Latin uses praescribat (command/prescribe); English renders as 'object', reversing the sense.
problems.fix: Let modesty, then, command these matters, even if the holy Scriptures cannot.
problems.ruling: praescribat means 'let modesty prescribe/command,' not 'object'; 'object' reverses the sense, as modesty should forbid, not protest.

edits.old: So it will not be objected that forbidden things should be watched.
edits.new: So it will not be commanded that the forbidden be watched.

edits.old: Let modesty, then, object on their behalf, even if the holy Scriptures cannot.
edits.new: Let modesty, then, command these matters, even if the holy Scriptures cannot.

fixed: Changed 'object on their behalf' to 'command these matters' to match praescribat.

problems.why: Same instrument list from opponents' argument, but different English word used two sections apart.
problems.fix: Use the same English word in both sections.

problems.why: Section 3's rebuttal of section 2's instrument list uses a different English word for the same instrument.
problems.fix: Use the same English word in both sections.

problems.quote: They often warn while they are forbidden.
problems.why: This sentence reverses the expected logic; it reads as a word-for-word gloss that does not make sense in English.
problems.fix: Rephrase, e.g. 'They often warn precisely by being forbidden.'

problems.quote: Having suffered shame, it forbade more because it was silent
problems.why: The subject 'it' (Scripture) 'suffering shame' is unclear and the clause reads like a literal translation that does not parse in English.
problems.fix: Rephrase, e.g. 'Out of modesty it forbade more by being silent.'

edits.old: Harps, lyres, flutes, tambourines, and citharas sang to God, not to an idol.
edits.new: Harps, cytherae, flutes, drums, and citharas sang to God, not to an idol.

edits.new: Out of modesty it forbade more by being silent, lest the truth, if it should descend even to these things, would have thought very badly about its faithful ones.

edits.old: They often warn while they are forbidden.
edits.new: They often warn precisely by being forbidden.

fixed: The instrument list in section 3 should match section 2's list. The source has 'nabla cynarae tibiae tympana et citharae' — nabla (harps), cynarae (cytherae), tibiae (flutes), tympana (drums), citharae (citharas). The English used 'lyres' for cynarae and 'tambourines' for tympana, which differ from section 2. Changed to 'cytherae' and 'drums' to match.

The source 'uerecundiam passa plus interdixit quia tacuit' means Scripture, having undergone modesty (i.e., out of modesty), forbade more by being silent. The English 'Having suffered shame' is unclear and misreads 'uerecundiam' as something Scripture suffers rather than the modesty it exercises. Changed to 'Out of modesty it forbade more by being silent.'

The source 'admonent saepe dum interdicuntur' means 'they often warn while they are being forbidden' — i.e., the very act of forbidding serves as a warning. The English 'They often warn while they are forbidden' is ambiguous and reads as a gloss. Changed to 'They often warn precisely by being forbidden.'

last_rejected.quote: So it will not be commanded that the forbidden be watched.
last_rejected.source_quote: non igitur praescribetur ut spectentur illicita
last_rejected.why: praescribetur here means 'an objection will not be raised'; context is opponents' legal-style objection, not a command.
last_rejected.fix: So no objection will be raised that the forbidden be watched.
last_rejected.ruling: praescribetur = will be prescribed/ordered; translation matches 'will not be commanded' (source: non igitur praescribetur ut spectentur illicita).

last_rejected.quote: Let modesty, then, command these matters
last_rejected.why: praescribat means 'let modesty raise its objection against them,' matching the legal-objection sense throughout.
last_rejected.fix: Let modesty, then, raise its objection against them
last_rejected.ruling: praescribat = let prescribe/command; rendering 'Let modesty … command' aligns with source (praescribat igitur istis pudor).

last_rejected.quote: They often warn while they are forbidden.
last_rejected.why: Subject is 'certain things' (quaedam), not 'they'; things 'warn while they are forbidden,' not people being warned.
last_rejected.fix: Certain things often warn while they are forbidden.
last_rejected.ruling: admonent = they warn; dum interdicuntur = while they are forbidden; translation conveys same sense despite pronoun ambiguity.
